items.title: L8: Planning around notice, checks and interim access
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; HMG Personnel Security Controls (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Several clocks run at once between an offer and a start: your notice period, the baseline checks, any vetting, and the department's own intake dates. The skill is to work out which clock actually controls your start and which decisions can safely wait.

Start with what is certain. Your notice period is set by your contract and is the earliest you can leave without breach. The baseline checks are usually the quickest to complete and depend mostly on how fast you return documents. Vetting at CTC, SC or DV takes longer and depends on the vetting service as well as you. Intake dates, where used, are fixed by the department.

Then identify the constraint. If your notice is long, it controls. If you have slow-to-find documents, they control. If the role needs higher clearance, vetting controls, unless the department will let you start on interim or restricted terms.

A useful rule is that you should only commit irreversibly when the controlling clock has stopped. For most people that means resigning after written confirmation that the conditions are met or that you can start, not on the strength of a likely date. Where you cannot wait, ask the department what risk remains and whether any date is guaranteed. A department cannot promise a clearance outcome, but it can say whether it will let you start before the decision.

If you are already in the Civil Service and moving departments, existing clearance may be transferable, but the new department decides whether it is adequate for the role, and it may need to be reviewed first. That can shorten the process, but do not assume it.

Always keep your own records: dates you sent documents, who confirmed what, and copies of written confirmations.

questions.prompt: Anil has a one-month notice period. The baseline checks will probably take two weeks, but the role needs SC vetting that has not started. Which clock is likely to control his start?

options.text: The department's intake date, which always overrides every other consideration
The baseline checks, because they are the first step and the others cannot start before they finish
His notice period, because it is the only date in the process he can control
The SC vetting, unless the department will let him start with restricted access while it is pending

questions.hint: Vetting is the longest and least controllable clock where the role needs it.

questions.prompt: Which action best fits the rule 'commit irreversibly only when the controlling clock has stopped'?

options.text: Resigning once he has written confirmation that the conditions are met or that he can start
Resigning as soon as the checks team says on the phone that the process is going well and should be quick
Resigning after the first one-to-one with his new manager, who has said that she expects to see him soon
Resigning on the day the offer is accepted, so that the maximum amount of notice can be given to his employer

questions.hint: Irreversible steps should wait for written confirmation.

questions.prompt: A department says it cannot promise an SC outcome, but it will let new starters begin with restricted access. What can the candidate reasonably take from this?

options.text: The clearance outcome is guaranteed once the person starts
The restricted access is permanent, whatever the vetting decision
The start may be possible before the decision, but the clearance outcome is not guaranteed
The department will cancel the vetting once the person has started

questions.hint: A start date is not an outcome promise.

questions.prompt: Bethan is moving from one department to another and holds SC. What is the sensible assumption about her clearance?

options.text: It is irrelevant, because each department grants its own clearance and ignores earlier ones
It may be transferable, but the new department decides whether it is adequate and whether a review is needed
It lapses the moment she leaves the old department, and a new application is always needed
It transfers automatically and cannot be questioned by the new department

questions.hint: Existing clearance can help, but the new sponsor decides.

questions.prompt: Which record is most useful to keep during the process?

options.text: The dates documents were sent and written confirmations of who agreed what
The vetting officer's private notes
A diary of the candidate's feelings about the process
A copy of the advert and nothing else

questions.hint: Your own dated records settle later disputes about timing.

questions.prompt: Which of these would most clearly be the 'constraint' for a candidate whose current contract needs three months' notice?

options.text: Whether the candidate has a passport
The department's choice of lunch venue for the first day
Their notice period, if the department's other steps take less time
The final interview date, which has already passed

questions.hint: If notice is the longest clock, it controls the start.

questions.prompt: A candidate cannot find an old tenancy agreement requested by the checks team. What is the sensible approach?

options.text: Make up a copy of the agreement from memory, so that something is sent on time and the check is not held up
Send an unrelated document that shows some other address and hope that it will be accepted instead
Wait until the agreement turns up, since the checkers will accept no other document to show an address
Tell the team now and offer other documents that show the address, such as bank statements

questions.hint: Early honesty with alternatives keeps the clock moving.

questions.prompt: Why might a department refuse to confirm a start date before checks are complete?

options.text: Because the law forbids any date being given before the first day
Because the conditions are not yet satisfied, and it cannot commit to employ someone it has not cleared
Because dates are confirmed only on the first Monday of each quarter
Because the line manager has not yet read the application

questions.hint: A date depends on the conditions being met.

questions.prompt: A start date moves back by a month because of delayed vetting. What should the candidate do about their notice?

options.text: Say nothing to either employer and hope for the best
Check the position with their current employer and the department, and agree any change in writing
Leave on the original date regardless, since the date was agreed with the department
Resign again in a month, as the first resignation no longer counts

questions.hint: Changes need to be agreed with both parties in writing.

questions.prompt: Which of these statements about clocks is most accurate?

options.text: The fastest step sets the start, since the others can run afterwards
All steps take the same time, so only the order matters
The slowest controllable-or-not step sets the earliest start, so identify it before planning
The candidate's own steps never affect the start

questions.hint: The earliest start is set by the slowest necessary step.

items.title: L8: Resolving conflicting identity evidence
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard; GOV.UK right to work guidance
items.body:
Real identity packs often contain tensions: a married name on one document and a birth name on another, an old address on a licence, a new passport with a different number, a surname spelled in two ways, or a date of birth that differs by a digit. The checker's job is not to reject these but to decide whether they can be explained and evidenced.

A good method is to ask three questions of each difference. What is the explanation? What document proves it? Could it be a sign of something else? A name change is explained by marriage and proved by a marriage certificate. A new passport number is explained by renewal and proved by the new passport. An old address on a licence is explained by a move and proved by recent bills or bank statements. A date of birth that differs by a digit is a typing error only if the original documents agree with each other; if two official documents differ, the issuing body may need to correct one.

Checks also look for patterns. One small difference is common. A set of differences with no explanation, or a document that looks altered, raises concern. The right response is to explain openly and offer evidence, not to adjust the documents or choose which version looks best.

Where the person's name differs between the passport and the right to work evidence, the employer must be satisfied the documents relate to the same person, and records how.

If a document is lost, a replacement or a letter from the issuing body may be accepted, depending on the department. Ask which alternatives they accept before relying on one.

The principle is consistency by explanation: every difference should have a reason that can be shown.

questions.prompt: A candidate's passport shows a middle name that does not appear on their bank statements. Which approach follows the three-question method?

options.text: Remove the middle name from the passport copy so that the documents agree
Change the bank's records before submitting the evidence
Say it is irrelevant and refuse to discuss it
Explain it, say what document shows the full name, and consider whether it could point to something else

questions.hint: Each difference needs an explanation and proof.

questions.prompt: A new passport has a different number from the old one. What explains it and what proves it?

options.text: Renewal explains it, and the new passport itself proves it
A move explains it, and a bill proves it
A typing error explains it, and a declaration proves it
A name change explains it, and a marriage certificate proves it

questions.hint: Passport numbers change on renewal.

questions.prompt: Two official documents show different dates of birth. What is the right conclusion?

options.text: The candidate may choose whichever of the two dates is more convenient and use it consistently from then on
The later of the two documents always overrides the earlier one, whatever the evidence behind each date
The difference is only a typing error by the issuer and can be ignored by the checker without further evidence
The issuing body may need to correct one of them, and the checker needs evidence of which is right

questions.hint: A conflict between official documents needs resolving at source.

questions.prompt: Which feature would raise the most concern in an identity pack?

options.text: A passport renewed since the first check
Several unexplained differences, or a document that looks altered
A surname that changed on marriage with a certificate supplied
A single address that has changed since the licence was issued

questions.hint: Patterns of unexplained differences and altered documents matter more than single explained ones.

questions.prompt: A candidate's driving licence has been lost and a replacement has not yet come. What should they do?

options.text: Ask the checks team which alternatives they accept, such as a letter from the issuing body or another photographic document
Send a photocopy of the lost licence and say nothing about its loss
Create a replacement document to look like the original
Wait until after starting, since the licence is not needed for the check

questions.hint: Check which alternatives the department accepts before relying on one.

questions.prompt: Why should a candidate never 'choose the version that looks best' when documents differ?

options.text: Because all versions are equally valid and so none can be preferred
Because choosing is the checker's job and not the candidate's
The checker is testing honesty and consistency, and choosing selectively looks like concealment
Because only the version on the passport is ever relevant

questions.hint: Selective presentation damages trust.

questions.prompt: An employer is looking at a passport name that differs from a share code record. What must it be satisfied of?

options.text: That the share code is correct, whatever the passport says
That the person has the same first name on both
That the documents relate to the same person, and it should record how it was satisfied
That the passport is correct, whatever the share code says

questions.hint: The employer must be satisfied the evidence relates to the person.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly matches an explanation and its proof?

options.text: Renewal of a passport explains a surname change, and the new passport itself proves it
Marriage explains a surname change, and a certificate proves it
A typing error explains a passport number, and a declaration proves it
A house move explains a date of birth difference, and a bill proves it

questions.hint: Explanations must be matched to suitable proof.

questions.prompt: A candidate discovers that their bank has spelled their surname with one letter wrong. What is the best step?

options.text: Mention it in a short note with the bank's confirmation or a corrected statement if available
Remove the bank statement from the pack and say nothing
Alter the statement by hand so that it matches the passport
Ignore it, since the bank's mistake does not concern the checker

questions.hint: Explain and evidence rather than alter or omit.

questions.prompt: What does 'consistency by explanation' mean?

options.text: Every document should be identical in every detail
Every explanation should be given verbally rather than in writing
Every difference should be removed before submission
Every difference should have a reason that can be shown

questions.hint: The aim is a coherent, evidenced account.

items.title: L8: Working out what a three-year window requires
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body:
The employment part of the BPSS usually looks back over the past three years. Applying that rule to a messy life takes a little reasoning. The window ends on the date you complete the form and runs back three years; everything in it must be accounted for, and anything wholly before it is outside the check, though some forms ask for longer histories for other purposes.

A period that straddles the start of the window is partly inside it. If you left a job 3 years and 2 months ago, the last two months of that job fall outside, but you still need to account for the period from the window's start onwards, so the previous job's dates are likely to matter. If you started a job two years ago and are still there, it covers the window from that point, and the earlier part of the window needs another entry.

Periods need not be employment. Study, travel, caring, illness and unemployment can all fill the window if you state them honestly. Overlaps are fine if genuine. Short gaps still need a label. Time abroad counts as time in the window like any other.

When unsure of a date, work from documents: a P60, a contract, a leaving letter or payslips. If these cannot be found, give a best estimate and say so.

If you complete the form some weeks before the department processes it, you may be asked to update it for anything that has changed since, such as a new job or a move. Keep a short log of changes after submission.

The common error is to treat the window as the last three jobs rather than the last three years.

questions.prompt: Dara's form is dated today. She left her last job exactly three years and one month ago and has been unemployed since. What does the window require her to account for?

options.text: Only the most recent three months, because shorter periods of unemployment are the ones that checkers query
Nothing at all, because her last job ended just outside the window and she has no employment inside it
Only the last job she held, because the check looks at the most recent employer however long ago she left it
The whole three years of unemployment, and probably the last job's end date too

questions.hint: The window is three years of time, so unemployment inside it must be accounted for.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes the window correctly?

options.text: It runs back three years from the date the form is completed, and every period inside it must be accounted for
It covers the last three jobs held, however long ago they ended and however short they were
It covers the last three years but only the periods in which the applicant was in paid work
It starts on the day the offer was accepted and runs back to the date of the advert

questions.hint: The window is three years of time, not three jobs.

questions.prompt: Why is treating the window as 'the last three jobs' an error?

options.text: Jobs are irrelevant to the check, which looks only at the places where a person has lived
The department prefers to see jobs listed in order of salary rather than in date order
A person may have held one job for ten years or six jobs in a year, and the check is about time rather than number of jobs
Three jobs is never enough for the department, which always asks for at least five employers

questions.hint: The window is measured in time.

questions.prompt: A candidate has been in the same job for two years and four months. What does the earlier part of the window need?

options.text: Nothing, because the current job is long enough to cover the whole window by itself
Another entry for the remaining eight months, such as a previous job, study or a period of unemployment
A short letter from the current employer saying that the earlier part of the window is not relevant
A promise to explain the earlier part at the first probation review once the new job has started

questions.hint: The whole three years needs covering.

questions.prompt: Which of these can legitimately fill part of the window?

options.text: Only periods in the UK, because overseas periods cannot be checked
Only periods of paid employment, because other periods cannot be evidenced
Study, travel, caring, illness or unemployment, honestly described
Only full-time study at a university, since other courses are not recognised

questions.hint: Any honest account of time can fill the window.

questions.prompt: A candidate submits the form and then starts a temporary job before the department processes it. What should they do?

options.text: Say nothing, because the form was correct on the day it was submitted and so remains correct
Tell the checks team, who may need to update the form for anything that has changed
Delete the job from their own records so that their notes match the submitted form
Wait until clearance is granted before mentioning it, so the new job cannot delay the process

questions.hint: Changes after submission should be reported.

questions.prompt: Which document is most useful for confirming job dates if memory is uncertain?

options.text: A contract, leaving letter, payslips or a P60
A reference written by the current manager about the person's general character
The original job advert, which gives the planned start date
A friend's recollection of when the job started

questions.hint: Documents give firmer dates than memory.

questions.prompt: A candidate cannot find any papers for a job. What should they do?

options.text: Leave the dates blank and let the checker choose suitable ones
Leave the job off the form, since a job with no papers cannot be checked
Pick dates that make the history look continuous, since gaps are what attract questions
Give a best estimate, mark it as approximate, and offer another way to confirm it

questions.hint: Estimates are fine if flagged.

questions.prompt: How should time spent abroad within the window be treated?

options.text: Described as unemployment, since that is simpler than naming a foreign employer
Accounted for like any other period, with the country and dates
Included only if the work abroad was paid, because unpaid time does not count
Left out, because overseas periods cannot be checked by a UK department

questions.hint: Time abroad counts in the window.

questions.prompt: Why does keeping a short log of changes after submission help?

options.text: It is a legal requirement that has to be kept for the rest of your career
It is sent automatically to the checks team each time you update it
It lets you give an accurate update quickly if the department asks
It replaces the original form once the department has processed it

questions.hint: A log makes updates easy and accurate.

items.title: L8: Conviction questions that depend on the form and the role
items.source: Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974 (legislation.gov.uk); HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard
items.body:
Whether you declare a conviction depends on three things taken together: whether the conviction is spent, whether the role is exempt from the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974, and what the form actually asks. Working through these in order avoids most mistakes.

First, is it spent? That depends on the sentence you received and how long has passed, under the Act's rules, which differ slightly across England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Some sentences never become spent. Second, is the role exempt? If it is not, a spent conviction is generally treated as if it had not happened, so the question is limited to unspent convictions. If it is exempt, the form may ask about spent convictions too, though some spent matters may be protected from disclosure under the exceptions rules. Third, read the exact wording: 'Do you have any unspent convictions?' differs from 'Have you ever been convicted?'. Answer what is asked.

Cautions are covered by similar logic, with their own rules.

If you are unsure whether something is spent, treat that uncertainty as a reason to check, not as permission to guess in your own favour. The checks team will normally tell you what the form means and where to find the rules.

When you declare, give the facts: what the conviction was for, when, the sentence, and a brief plain account. Do not minimise or add excuses. If circumstances have changed since, say so briefly.

A declaration made on a form is not repeated casually elsewhere. If you realise later that you answered wrongly, tell the checks team promptly and correct it.

Finally, a conviction is not automatically fatal. Honesty and relevance are what are weighed.

questions.prompt: Which order best captures the reasoning about declaring a conviction?

options.text: First whether it is spent, then whether the role is exempt, then exactly what the form asks
First whether the role is senior, since senior roles always require everything to be declared
First ask a friend, then decide in the way that seems fairest
First what the form asks, and then whether it is spent only if the form seems unclear

questions.hint: The three questions together decide the answer.

questions.prompt: The role is not exempt and the form asks about 'any unspent convictions'. Fatima has a spent conviction. What does she write?

options.text: She writes that she has an unspent conviction, which avoids a long explanation of the sentence
She declares it anyway to be on the safe side, even though the question does not ask for it
She leaves the question blank, since she cannot be certain which answer is the right one
She answers the question as asked and does not declare the spent conviction

questions.hint: The question defines what is declared for a non-exempt role.

questions.prompt: The form asks 'Have you ever been convicted of an offence?' for an exempt role. How does that differ from asking about unspent convictions?

options.text: It is the same question, because the word 'ever' makes no difference
It applies only to offences committed in the workplace, not to offences in private life
It covers only the last three years, in line with the baseline employment check
It can include spent convictions, so the answer may differ, though some matters may be protected

questions.hint: Wording and exemption together widen what may be asked.

questions.prompt: Gareth cannot remember the sentence he received and is unsure whether a conviction is spent. What is the best approach?

options.text: Declare it only if a friend who knows the law says it is unspent
Treat the uncertainty as a reason to check the rules or ask the checks team, not to guess in his own favour
Declare nothing and see whether the checker raises it, since the form can be corrected later
Assume it is spent, since most old convictions are by now and he would rather not draw attention

questions.hint: Uncertainty is a prompt to check, not a licence to guess.

questions.prompt: Which content is most useful in a short declaration?

options.text: What it was for, when it happened, the sentence, and a brief plain account
A long explanation of why the court's decision was wrong and unfair
The names of the other people involved in the offence, to show the full picture
A request that the matter be ignored because it was a long time ago

questions.hint: Facts, plainly stated, are what the department needs.

questions.prompt: Why should a declaration avoid excuses and minimising?

options.text: Minimising shortens the rehabilitation period, which the rules do not allow
Excuses are an offence under the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act and can lead to prosecution
A plain account reads as honest, whereas excuses suggest the person has not accepted the facts
The department deletes any declaration that contains an excuse and treats it as incomplete

questions.hint: A plain account carries more credibility.

questions.prompt: After submitting, Ines realises that she gave a wrong answer about a caution. What should she do?

options.text: Say nothing, because the mistake was unintentional and so cannot count against her
Wait for the vetting officer to find it, since the form has gone and cannot now be changed
Tell the checks team promptly and correct it
Ask a colleague to amend the form on her behalf

questions.hint: Prompt correction shows honesty.

questions.prompt: Which statement about cautions is correct?

options.text: They are the same as convictions in every respect, including when they become spent
They never matter, because a caution is not a conviction
They matter only for roles that are exempt from the Act
They follow similar logic, with their own rules about when they become spent

questions.hint: Cautions have their own timing rules.

questions.prompt: Where might some spent matters still be protected from disclosure even for an exempt role?

options.text: Under the exceptions rules, which can filter certain old or minor matters
Only for applicants under twenty-five, who are treated differently
Only in Scotland, where the Act does not apply
Nowhere, since an exempt role may ask about anything at all

questions.hint: The exceptions rules can filter some matters.

questions.prompt: Which view about a declared conviction is most accurate?

options.text: It is ignored once declared, since it was disclosed voluntarily
It is not automatically fatal, and honesty and relevance are weighed
It always ends the application, whatever the circumstances
It is decided by the applicant's current manager, who knows the applicant best

questions.hint: The process is a judgement, not an automatic bar.

items.title: L8: Three gates: right to work, nationality and clearance
items.source: GOV.UK: Check a job applicant's right to work; Civil Service Nationality Rules; HMG Personnel Security Controls
items.body:
A candidate for a Civil Service post may need to pass three separate gates. The right to work gate asks whether the law lets them work for this employer. The nationality gate asks whether this post is open to people of their status, as set out in the advert's eligibility statement. The clearance gate asks whether they can be trusted with the access the role involves, for roles that need vetting above the baseline.

Passing one gate does not pass the others. A person with settled status has the right to work, but a post reserved for UK nationals is still closed. A UK national with the right to work may still be refused clearance. A person cleared at SC in one role may meet the nationality rules for that role but not for another with a narrower statement.

To diagnose a problem, ask which gate it is at. If the issue is a lack of documents showing status, it is the right to work gate and the remedy is evidence. If the issue is the advert's wording, it is the nationality gate and the remedy is to apply for a post that is open to the candidate, or to ask the contact in the advert. If the issue is a vetting concern, it is the clearance gate, and the remedy is a full and honest account and, if refused, the review route.

Dual nationality can touch the nationality gate and the clearance gate: an advert may be open to dual nationals, yet vetting may consider the links. Time abroad can touch the clearance gate through checkable history.

Do not try to solve a problem at one gate with evidence relevant to another.

questions.prompt: A person with settled status applies for a post reserved to UK nationals. Which gate stops them?

options.text: The right to work gate, because settled status is not enough on its own
The clearance gate, since vetting always decides eligibility before the other checks
The nationality gate, even though they have passed the right to work gate
None, because settled status covers every post in the Civil Service

questions.hint: Passing one gate does not pass the others.

questions.prompt: A UK national with the right to work has an application for SC clearance refused. Which gate is involved?

options.text: The right to work gate, because a refusal means the status documents were wrong
The nationality gate, because a refusal shows the person is not eligible to apply
All three gates equally, since a refusal at one means a failure at all of them
The clearance gate

questions.hint: Clearance is separate from the other two.

questions.prompt: A candidate cannot show documents proving their immigration status. Which gate is this, and what is the remedy?

options.text: None, because documents are needed only after the first day
The right to work gate, and the remedy is evidence
The clearance gate, and the remedy is an appeal to the vetting service
The nationality gate, and the remedy is to apply for a different post

questions.hint: The remedy follows from the gate.

questions.prompt: An advert says 'UK nationals only' and a candidate holds two other nationalities but no UK one. What is the correct step?

options.text: Apply for posts that are open to them, or ask the contact in the advert if unsure
Provide more documents proving the right to work, which will satisfy the statement
Seek an early review of any clearance decision, since that will override the statement
Apply anyway, since eligibility statements are guidance that selection panels can waive

questions.hint: Wording problems are nationality gate problems.

questions.prompt: Why is it unhelpful to answer a nationality problem with extra right to work evidence?

options.text: Right to work evidence is never accepted by the Civil Service in any circumstances
Nationality is decided by the Home Office, which does not consult employers
It answers a different question from the one the advert is asking
Extra evidence is never needed once the first check has been done

questions.hint: Evidence must match the gate.

questions.prompt: An advert is open to dual nationals. Which gate might still raise a question?

options.text: The nationality gate again, since it is applied a second time at vetting
The clearance gate, because vetting may consider the links
The right to work gate, because dual nationals are not allowed to work in government
Neither gate, since an advert open to dual nationals guarantees clearance

questions.hint: Vetting may weigh foreign links.

questions.prompt: Time spent living abroad can most directly affect which gate?

options.text: The nationality gate, through the length of residence required in the advert
The right to work gate, through the date of arrival in the UK
None, since time abroad is never recorded
The clearance gate, through the amount of checkable history

questions.hint: Checkable history is a vetting question.

questions.prompt: A candidate holds SC from one role and applies to a different post with a narrower eligibility statement. What is true?

options.text: They may meet the nationality rules for the first post but not for the new one
They must give up their existing clearance before they apply
They are automatically eligible for the new post, because SC is the higher check
Their existing clearance becomes void as soon as they apply

questions.hint: Statements differ between posts.

questions.prompt: A candidate is refused vetting. What is the sensible next step?

options.text: Present fresh right to work documents, which will reopen the decision
Ask for the reasons and use the review route, giving a full and honest account
Ask the nationality contact to change the advert so that the refusal does not apply
Reapply to the same role immediately, with the same information

questions.hint: The remedy for a clearance problem is the clearance review route.

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarises the three gates?

options.text: They are the same test applied three times by different bodies
They are applied in order, and failure at the first cancels the rest
They are decided by one person at one time
They are separate, and passing one does not pass the others

questions.hint: Each gate answers a different question.

items.title: L8: Deciding the level when access is complicated
items.source: HMG Personnel Security Controls (GOV.UK); Government Security Classifications Policy
items.body:
Most examples of choosing a clearance level are simple: regular access to SECRET, SC. Real roles are more mixed. Sponsors look at what the person can reach, how often, whether they are supervised, and what harm they could do.

Frequency and supervision matter. Occasional, supervised access to sensitive material usually needs less than regular, unsupervised access. A visitor who is escorted at all times and sees nothing sensitive may need no clearance at all, while a cleaner with unescorted access to secure areas out of hours may need a check, because the risk comes from being present and unobserved.

Systems access matters. Administrators who can reach, copy or alter large amounts of data can pose more risk than a user who reads a few documents. A role that holds privileged access to a database of personal records may need more than a role that reads a single OFFICIAL file, even though the classification of each record is low.

Context matters. The same document may be low risk in one department and high risk in another. A post in a high-threat location, or with proximity to people at risk, can justify a check such as CTC even if little classified information is involved.

The sponsor should choose the lowest level that manages the risk. Over-requesting wastes time and intrudes; under-requesting leaves a gap. The wrong answer is to copy the level from the last post or to pick by grade. If a role changes, review the level.

If you hold clearance and your duties grow, tell your manager, because the level may no longer match the access.

questions.prompt: A cleaner has unescorted access to secure areas out of hours but sees no documents. Why might a check still be needed?

options.text: Cleaning is a protected category under the Official Secrets Act
Cleaners are always cleared to DV because of their access to every part of a building
The risk comes from being present and unobserved in a sensitive area
The cleaner may read papers left on desks, which would always be a deliberate breach

questions.hint: Access and observation matter, not only reading.

questions.prompt: Why might a system administrator need a higher level than someone who reads a few SECRET files?

options.text: The administrator can reach, copy or alter large amounts of data, so the potential harm is greater
Administrators handle only OFFICIAL data, which needs a higher level of care
Administrators are always more senior than the people whose files they manage
The level depends on the person's job title, and administrators have a longer one

questions.hint: Reach and potential harm matter.

questions.prompt: A visitor is escorted at all times and sees nothing sensitive. What is the likely requirement?

options.text: Baseline checks in every case, whatever the access
DV, because anyone entering a government building needs the highest level
Possibly no clearance, because escort and limited access manage the risk
CTC, because visitors in a secure building are always treated as a terrorist risk

questions.hint: Supervision can replace the need for a check.

questions.prompt: A role has little classified material but involves close proximity to people at risk of attack. Which level might fit?

options.text: CTC
DV, because proximity to people at risk always needs the highest level
Baseline only, because nothing in the role is classified
SC, because a risk to people is treated as a risk to SECRET material

questions.hint: Proximity risk can justify CTC.

questions.prompt: Why is copying the clearance level from the last post a poor method?

options.text: The last holder's clearance is a personal matter and must not be reused
Levels cannot be copied between posts, because each has its own reference number
The last post's level is always too high, because posts accumulate responsibilities
The access, supervision and context may differ, so the risk may differ

questions.hint: Each role needs its own assessment.

questions.prompt: Which approach best fits 'lowest level that manages the risk'?

options.text: Choose the highest level available, to be on the safe side
Choose the level the access justifies, no higher and no lower
Choose the lowest level available, whatever the access involved
Choose the level held by the line manager, so that the team is consistent

questions.hint: Proportionate and sufficient.

questions.prompt: You hold SC and your duties grow to include regular access to TOP SECRET material. What should you do?

options.text: Apply to the vetting service yourself, since only the holder can request a review
Wait for the next scheduled review, since levels change only at review dates
Tell your manager, since the level may no longer match the access
Say nothing, since SC already covers all access to TOP SECRET material

questions.hint: Changes in access should be flagged.

questions.prompt: Two posts handle the same document, but in one the holder is supervised and in the other is not. What follows?

options.text: The supervised post may need less, because supervision manages part of the risk of misuse
They need the same level of clearance, since the document that is handled is the same in both posts
The unsupervised post needs less, because staff who work unsupervised are assumed to be trusted more
Neither needs any check at all, since the document is held in a secure place that only cleared staff enter

questions.hint: Supervision and frequency matter.

questions.prompt: What is the main drawback of over-requesting clearance?

options.text: It has no drawback, since a higher level always gives more protection
It wastes time and money and intrudes more than the risk requires
It makes the application faster, because the vetting service prioritises senior levels
It makes the person more secure, which creates a conflict with data protection

questions.hint: Intrusion and delay.

questions.prompt: What risk follows from asking for a clearance level that is too low for the role?

options.text: It increases the cost of the vetting for the department
It makes the person ineligible for the right to work
It makes the process longer for the candidate
It leaves part of the risk to sensitive assets unmanaged

questions.hint: Under-requesting leaves risk unmanaged.

items.title: L8: Residence, foreign links and what to put on the form
items.source: UK Security Vetting guidance; HMG Personnel Security Controls (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Vetting wants to be able to check a person's history, and that is easier where they have lived and worked in the UK for a continuous period. For each level there is an expectation of a period of UK residence, and the period rises with the level. This does not mean that anyone who has lived abroad is excluded. It means the vetting service has to be able to verify enough of your history to be confident, and where records are thin, it may take longer, need more evidence, or lead to a decision at a lower level for the role.

If you have lived abroad, give the dates, the places and what you were doing, with whatever evidence you have: employers, schools, tenancy records, travel documents, referees who knew you at the time. If an overseas record is hard to obtain, say so rather than leaving a gap.

Foreign links are considered in their context. Family abroad, a partner of another nationality, property, financial interests and regular contact with people overseas are all normal in modern life. Vetting asks where the links are, how close they are, and whether they could be used for pressure. Links to countries that pose a risk to UK interests will be looked at more closely, but are not an automatic bar.

What to put on the form: include the link, how you know the person or place, and how often you are in contact. If you are unsure whether to include something, include it with a short explanation. Do not assume that a link is irrelevant because it is innocent.

After clearance, report significant changes, such as a new partner abroad or a plan to move overseas for a long period.

questions.prompt: Why is continuous UK residence relevant to vetting?

options.text: It is relevant only to pay, since overseas time is paid differently
It is required by the right to work rules for every Civil Service post
It proves that the person is a British citizen, which is required for all clearance
It makes a person's history easier to verify, and the expected period rises with the level

questions.hint: Verification is the purpose.

questions.prompt: Roya has lived abroad for several years and has few UK records. What is a likely effect?

options.text: Her time abroad is ignored, since vetting looks only at UK records
Vetting may take longer, need more evidence, or lead to a decision at a lower level for the role
She is automatically refused, since clearance requires continuous UK residence
She is automatically cleared, since time abroad cannot be held against anyone

questions.hint: Thin records limit verification.

questions.prompt: What should Roya do about an overseas record that is hard to obtain?

options.text: Leave a gap in her history, since the vetting service will not expect overseas detail
Ask a friend in the UK to confirm the period without having seen it
Say so, and offer other evidence such as referees, tenancy records or travel documents
Invent a plausible record, so that the history is complete

questions.hint: Be open and offer alternatives.

questions.prompt: A candidate has a brother living abroad and a small business interest overseas. How does vetting treat links like these?

options.text: In context, asking how close they are and whether they could be a route to pressure
As irrelevant to clearance, which is why applicants are usually advised not to mention them on the form
As an automatic bar to any clearance above the baseline
As relevant only at DV level, where family and business interests are always examined in full detail

questions.hint: Context decides.

questions.prompt: Which is the best approach when unsure if a link is worth mentioning?

options.text: Ask a friend to decide whether it matters
Mention it only if asked about it at interview
Leave it out, since innocent links are of no interest to vetting
Include it with a short explanation

questions.hint: Include and explain.

questions.prompt: Why is it wrong to assume that an innocent link is irrelevant?

options.text: The vetting officer, not the applicant, decides what matters, and a missing link may look like concealment
Every link is a security risk, however innocent it may be
Innocent links are rare, so any link needs to be explained
Links are always investigated by the police before clearance is granted

questions.hint: Disclosure is for the vetting officer to weigh.

questions.prompt: Which details are useful about a foreign link?

options.text: Only the person's name, since other details are private
Nothing, since details are not needed once a link is mentioned
How you know the person or place, and how often you are in contact
Only the country, since the vetting service looks up the rest

questions.hint: Context makes links assessable.

questions.prompt: Which statement about links to countries that pose a risk to UK interests is correct?

options.text: They are ignored, as vetting treats all countries alike
They will be looked at more closely, but are not an automatic bar
They are examined at DV only, and not at lower levels
They bar a person from every level of clearance

questions.hint: Closer scrutiny, not automatic exclusion.

questions.prompt: After clearance, which change should you report?

options.text: A new mobile phone contract, since the number has changed
A plan to move overseas for a long period, or a new close relationship abroad
A change of gym, since you may meet new people there
A change of internet provider at home, since it may affect security

questions.hint: Significant changes relevant to risk are reported.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the expected residence period?

options.text: It is the same for every level of clearance, so that all clearances can be compared with one another
It is chosen by each candidate, who simply states for how long they have lived in the UK
It rises with the level, and the aim is to allow checking, not to exclude
It applies to the baseline checks only, and is not used at the higher levels of clearance at all

questions.hint: Level and verification link.

items.title: L8: Deciding handling when material is mixed
items.source: Government Security Classifications Policy (GOV.UK); ICO guidance on personal data
items.body:
Real work seldom produces neat documents. An email chain may mix policy discussion with customer details; a briefing may combine public figures with a commercial secret; a report may be built from a dozen sources. Deciding how to handle such material means thinking about the harm if the whole thing were lost, not about the least sensitive part.

Two working rules help. First, a compiled document takes the handling needs of its most sensitive content, and may need more than any single part because of aggregation. A table that brings together scattered facts can reveal something none of them reveals alone. Second, when you forward or quote from a source, you carry its handling needs with you. Copying a paragraph from a sensitive paper into a new note does not make the note less sensitive.

To decide, ask: what is the most sensitive thing in this? Who needs to see it? What harm if it reached the wrong people? Then apply the controls for that, such as OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE handling, a restricted distribution list, or secure sharing in place of attachments. Where you cannot tell, ask the owner of the information.

Removing the sensitive part may be an option. A summary that omits personal data may be shareable more widely, but check that it cannot be linked back, because small numbers or unusual details can identify individuals.

When replying to a long chain, check who is on it and what is in the earlier messages before you press send. Many accidental disclosures come from a reply that carries old content to a new recipient.

Record decisions where practice requires, so that colleagues handling the material later know the basis.

questions.prompt: An email chain mixes policy discussion with one customer's medical details. How should the chain be handled?

options.text: As TOP SECRET, because any medical detail raises the whole chain to the highest level
As ordinary OFFICIAL with no special care, because most of the chain is policy discussion
As public, because the policy part is not sensitive and the medical details are only one customer's
With the care the medical details need, since the most sensitive content sets the handling

questions.hint: The most sensitive content sets the handling.

questions.prompt: Why might a table combining scattered facts need more care than any of the facts alone?

options.text: Aggregation can reveal something that none of the facts shows by itself
Tables are always classified one level higher than the text from which they were taken
Tables take longer to send, and delay itself increases the risk
The facts become inaccurate when they are combined, so the table has to be protected

questions.hint: Compilation can create new sensitivity.

questions.prompt: You copy a paragraph from a sensitive paper into a new note. What follows?

options.text: The note carries the handling needs of the source paragraph
The note becomes public, because you are the author of the new text
The note has no handling needs, since it is a new document that you have written
The note must be destroyed immediately, since copying is never allowed

questions.hint: Handling needs travel with content.

questions.prompt: Which is the best first question in deciding how to handle a mixed document?

options.text: Which part of it is the longest?
Who wrote most of it?
What is the most sensitive thing in it?
Which part of it was written first?

questions.hint: Start from the most sensitive content.

questions.prompt: You cannot tell how sensitive some information is. What should you do?

options.text: Treat it as public until someone objects, since the owner would have marked it otherwise
Share it widely so that more people can judge how sensitive it is
Mark it TOP SECRET yourself and lock it away to be safe
Ask the owner of the information and treat it with care in the meantime

questions.hint: The owner decides the classification.

questions.prompt: A summary omits the personal data from a report. What should the author check before sharing it widely?

options.text: That the summary has the same title as the original report
That small numbers or unusual details cannot identify individuals
That the summary is shorter than the report that it summarises
That the summary has been signed by the author of the original

questions.hint: Removal may not be enough if details identify people.

questions.prompt: Before replying to a long email chain, what should you check?

options.text: The time the chain started, in case the subject has changed
The spelling of the subject line, so that it is professional
Only the last message, since that is the one to which you are replying
Who is on it, and what the earlier messages contain

questions.hint: Replies carry old content to new recipients.

questions.prompt: Which is a good alternative to attaching a sensitive file to an email?

options.text: Attaching it to several separate emails in parts, so that no single message holds it all
A secure sharing route, with access limited to those who need it
Sending it to a personal account first and then forwarding it on
Printing it and leaving it on a colleague's desk for them to find

questions.hint: Controlled sharing is safer.

questions.prompt: Why record a handling decision where practice requires it?

options.text: Records are always made public so the decision can be checked by outsiders
The decision becomes a legal contract once it is written down
Colleagues who handle the material later can see the basis
The decision lasts for one year unless a record is kept

questions.hint: Records help consistency.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the principle for mixed material?

options.text: Think about the harm if the whole thing were lost, not just the least sensitive part
Handle it according to its author, since authors know best
Handle it according to its length, since longer documents carry more risk
Handle it according to its least sensitive part, since that is most of it

questions.hint: The most sensitive content drives handling.

items.title: L8: Triage after a security or data incident
items.source: ICO guidance on personal data breaches; HMG security incident guidance (GOV.UK)
items.body:
When something goes wrong, the order of your actions matters more than their number. A sensible sequence is: stop, report, contain, record, then learn.

Stop means halting what you were doing so as not to make it worse: not forwarding the email again, not wiping the device, not deleting evidence. Report means telling the right people at once through the department's route, usually your line manager and the security or data protection team. Do this first and fast, because the clock for notifying the Information Commissioner's Office, generally 72 hours from awareness where a breach is likely to risk individuals, starts when the organisation becomes aware, and your report is how it becomes aware.

Contain means limiting the spread under the direction of the responsible team: asking a recipient to delete a message, remotely locking a device, changing a password. Record means noting what happened, when you noticed, who was affected and what was done, factually and without speculation. Learn means a review afterwards to prevent a repeat, in a culture that treats honest reporting as responsible.

Assessing severity is not your job alone, but it helps to know the factors: how sensitive the data is, how many people are affected, whether it was seen by someone outside the organisation, whether it was encrypted, and what harm could follow. A lost, encrypted laptop is very different from an unencrypted spreadsheet sent to a stranger.

If the incident involves a suspected hostile approach, a lost pass or a device that may have been tampered with, report it as a security incident as well, since it can affect others.

Do not try to hide a mistake, and do not investigate it yourself. The cover-up is usually worse than the error.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best reflects how to respond to an incident?

options.text: Contain it alone, then report a week later if it has not been resolved
Learn, record, contain, report, then stop
Record, delete, report, then forget
Stop, report, contain, record, then learn

questions.hint: Order matters in incident response.

questions.prompt: After sending an email to the wrong recipient, which action should you not take first?

options.text: Try to fix it quietly and report it later
Stop forwarding the email any further
Note the time at which you noticed the mistake
Tell your line manager and the data protection team

questions.hint: Report first and fast.

questions.prompt: Why does an early internal report matter for the ICO deadline?

options.text: The deadline is paused until the individual has finished their own investigation
The deadline starts when the incident happens, whatever anyone knows about it
The clock generally starts when the organisation becomes aware, and your report is how it becomes aware
The deadline is set by the individual who made the mistake, who can choose its length

questions.hint: Awareness starts the clock.

questions.prompt: Which combination would make a data loss most serious?

options.text: A few non-sensitive records, sent to a colleague inside the organisation who also has a right to see them
Unencrypted data about many people, sent to someone outside the organisation by mistake
Encrypted data on a locked laptop that is found within the hour
Data that the department itself has already published on its own website for anyone to read

questions.hint: Severity depends on sensitivity, number, exposure and protection.

questions.prompt: What does 'containment' mean in responding to an incident?

options.text: Limiting the spread of the problem, under the direction of the responsible team
Establishing who was to blame, so that action can be taken
Writing the final report about the incident for the department
Closing the incident record once it has been reported

questions.hint: Containment limits harm.

questions.prompt: Which record is most useful after an incident?

options.text: A copy of the email sent to the press office, in case of questions
A note of how the person felt, so that the department understands the stress
A note of who the person thinks was at fault, based on what they have heard
A factual note of what happened, when it was noticed, who was affected and what was done

questions.hint: Facts, not speculation.

questions.prompt: Which action risks destroying evidence?

options.text: Noting the time and place at which the device was last seen
Wiping a device that may have been tampered with, before security staff have looked at it
Leaving the device switched off until it is collected
Reporting the device as lost as soon as the loss is noticed

questions.hint: Do not wipe devices without direction.

questions.prompt: You think you were approached by someone trying to obtain information about your work. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the person for their name and leave it at that
Mention it to a friend who works in another department
Report it as a security incident through the security route
Handle it yourself and say nothing, since no information was given

questions.hint: Hostile approaches should be reported.

questions.prompt: Why is it a poor idea to investigate your own mistake before reporting it?

options.text: It can disturb evidence and delays proper handling by the responsible team
It leads to automatic dismissal, since staff may not investigate themselves
It is a criminal offence for the person who made the mistake
It makes the incident public, since investigating leaves a visible trace

questions.hint: The responsible team should investigate.

questions.prompt: How does a good security culture treat honest reporting?

options.text: As an admission of guilt, which has to be followed by a penalty
As a matter for the police in every case
As unimportant, since most incidents are minor
As responsible behaviour, followed by learning rather than automatic blame

questions.hint: Reporting is encouraged.

items.title: L8: Disclosure dilemmas: who may be told what
items.source: Official Secrets Act 1989; Civil Service Code; Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 (legislation.gov.uk)
items.body:
Dilemmas about disclosure are rarely a simple choice between silence and publication. Several routes exist, and the skill is to pick the right one.

Start with whether the matter is a concern about wrongdoing or just a wish to talk. If you simply want to describe your job, general terms are fine. If you are being asked for information, whether by a journalist, a friend, a former colleague or a supplier, the question is whether you are authorised to give it. Authority usually comes from your role and your department's rules, not from a personal judgement that the information is harmless.

If the matter is a concern about something improper, the Civil Service Code route applies: your line manager or senior colleague, a nominated officer, then the Civil Service Commission. The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protects proper disclosures and does not override the Official Secrets Act. The 1989 Act has no public interest defence, so a belief that disclosure serves the public does not make it lawful.

If a request arrives through the Freedom of Information Act 2000, it goes to the specialist team, and you should not alter or delete the information. If it arrives from a former colleague who now works for a company, remember that they remain bound by the Act and by their own duties, and that you owe them no more than you would any outsider.

If you think you have already disclosed something you should not have, tell your manager at once. Early reporting allows damage limitation and is treated much better than discovery.

Finally, regard the duty as continuing: it does not end when the project ends or when you leave.

questions.prompt: A former colleague, now working for a supplier, asks about a forthcoming department decision. What is the right approach?

options.text: Share it, if they promise to keep it confidential and not to pass it to anyone else at the supplier
Treat the request as you would one from any outsider, and do not share anything unreleased
Share it, because they know the context and used to work for the department
Share only the parts of it that are already known inside the team and are unlikely to cause harm

questions.hint: A former colleague has no special entitlement.

questions.prompt: Which question is most important when you are asked for information?

options.text: Whether the information is interesting to them
Whether you can remember it accurately
Whether you are authorised to give it
Whether the person asking is polite and friendly

questions.hint: Authority, not harmlessness, decides.

questions.prompt: Why does a belief that disclosure is in the public interest not make it lawful under the 1989 Act?

options.text: The belief must be shared by two people before the Act allows it
The Act contains no public interest defence
The Act applies only to ministers, and so the belief of other staff is irrelevant
The public interest is always served by secrecy, so a contrary belief is a mistake

questions.hint: No public interest defence.

questions.prompt: You think something improper is happening in your team. Which route applies first?

options.text: The Civil Service Code route, starting with your line manager or a nominated officer
A newspaper, because publicity is the quickest way to stop it
A social media post, because it can reach senior management quickly
Your local councillor, who can raise it with the department

questions.hint: Internal routes come first.

questions.prompt: How does the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 relate to the Official Secrets Act?

options.text: It applies instead of the Official Secrets Act for civil servants
It has no connection with disclosures at all
It protects proper disclosures but does not override the Official Secrets Act
It cancels the Official Secrets Act for anyone who makes a disclosure

questions.hint: The Acts operate together.

questions.prompt: You realise that you told a friend something you should not have. What is the best step?

options.text: Wait to see whether the friend repeats it, since it may never matter
Ask the friend to forget it and say nothing more to anyone
Delete the messages you sent to the friend, so that there is no record
Tell your manager at once so that damage can be limited

questions.hint: Early reporting is treated better than discovery.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the duty of confidentiality is correct?

options.text: It applies only while you are on duty and not outside working hours
It is continuing and does not end when a project ends or when you leave
It ends when the project it relates to has finished
It ends when your probation ends and your appointment is confirmed

questions.hint: The duty continues.

questions.prompt: An FOI request asks for a draft you wrote. What should you do?

options.text: Pass it to the specialist team and keep the draft unaltered
Rewrite the draft so that it reads better before it is released
Delete the draft before the team sees it, since drafts are not final
Ignore the request, since drafts are not covered by the Act

questions.hint: Preserve and pass on.

questions.prompt: Which is a sign that a person is relying on 'harmlessness' rather than authority?

options.text: They consult their manager before replying
They check with the owner of the information
They ask the press office what they may say
They say 'it is not secret, really' and share it without checking

questions.hint: Authority comes from the role and rules.

questions.prompt: Where should a journalist's request for comment on a story about your department be sent?

options.text: To a colleague in another department who has dealt with the press before
To your own personal email, so that you can reply in your own time
To the press office, with your manager informed
To the person who wrote the story, so that they can pass it on

questions.hint: Press contact goes through the press office.

items.title: L8: Layered conflicts: relationships, jobs and gifts
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code; Bribery Act 2010
items.body:
Conflicts rarely come singly. A single situation may involve a relationship, an outside interest and an offer of hospitality, and the way you handle the first can affect the others.

The approach is to list the interests, decide which could affect your work, declare them together, and let the department decide how to manage them. Relationships at work include close personal relationships with a colleague you manage or whose pay or performance you influence. The usual rule is to declare it, and the department may change reporting lines so that you are not making decisions about each other. Concealing a relationship that affects decisions is the issue, not the relationship.

Outside employment may need approval and can be refused if it conflicts with your duties, takes too much time, or uses official information. Directorships and shareholdings are declared. Voluntary roles, such as being a school governor, are usually fine but are declared if they could connect with your work.

Gifts and hospitality are assessed on value, purpose, timing and the giver's interest in your decisions. A modest item at the end of a project is different from an offer during a live procurement, or from repeated offers by the same supplier. Record offers whether you accept or not.

Where several interests overlap, such as a family member who works for a supplier who also offers you hospitality, treat the combination as more serious than each alone and declare early.

A declared interest that has been managed is not a mark against you. An undeclared one that comes to light is.

Review your declarations when your role or personal circumstances change, because a past declaration may not cover the new situation.

questions.prompt: You start a close relationship with someone you manage. What is the usual correct step?

options.text: Declare it so that the department can change reporting lines if needed
Give your colleague a better appraisal to avoid any awkwardness between you
End your management role without telling anyone why
Keep it private, since a personal relationship is not connected to work

questions.hint: The issue is concealing a relationship that affects decisions.

questions.prompt: Which outside role would normally be declared if it could connect with your work?

options.text: Attending a weekly evening class in a subject that has nothing to do with your department's work
A voluntary role such as school governor, where there is a link to your work
Walking a neighbour's dog on some weekday evenings when they are away for work
Playing in a local band at weekends, for which you are paid a small fee at community events

questions.hint: Voluntary roles are declared if there is a link.

questions.prompt: A family member works for a supplier that also offers you hospitality. How should you treat this?

options.text: As two small matters, neither of which needs a declaration
As the family member's matter only, since hospitality is offered to many people
As more serious than each matter alone, and declare it early
As a reason to refuse all hospitality in future without telling anyone

questions.hint: Combinations raise the level of concern.

questions.prompt: Which factor would make a gift more concerning?

options.text: It is a branded pen handed out at a meeting
It is a small item given at the end of a project
It is shared among the whole team and recorded
It is offered during a live procurement by a supplier with an interest in your decisions

questions.hint: Timing and the giver's interest matter.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of a declared interest that has been managed?

options.text: It lowers your clearance level by one step
It must be repeated every week
It ends your career in the department
It is not a mark against you

questions.hint: Declaring is correct behaviour.

questions.prompt: When should you review your declarations?

options.text: Only when you are asked to by an audit
When your role or personal circumstances change
Every year on the same date, whatever has changed
Never, since a declaration made once covers every future role

questions.hint: Old declarations may not cover new situations.

questions.prompt: Which statement about outside employment is correct?

options.text: It is always allowed, provided it is outside normal hours
It is allowed without approval if it is unpaid
It may need approval and can be refused if it conflicts with your duties
It is never allowed, whatever the job involves

questions.hint: Approval and conflict are the tests.

questions.prompt: What should you do with offers of gifts you refuse?

options.text: Record them in line with local rules
Say nothing, since nothing was accepted
Report them to the police in every case
Destroy any note you have made, so that there is no trace

questions.hint: Recording helps spot patterns.

questions.prompt: Which approach best handles a situation with several interests?

options.text: Declare them only after you are asked
Declare none of them, since each is minor on its own
List them, decide which could affect your work, declare them together, and let the department decide
Declare only the smallest interest, so that the form is simple

questions.hint: Declare together and let the department manage.

questions.prompt: Why is a concealed relationship that affects decisions worse than the relationship itself?

options.text: Concealment prevents the department from managing the effect on decisions
Relationships at work are forbidden, so any relationship is a breach
Concealment is an offence under the Official Secrets Act
Relationships always affect decisions, so they must be ended

questions.hint: The harm is the lack of openness.

items.title: L8: Judging probation situations
items.source: Civil Service Management Code; Civil Service Code; Equality Act 2010
items.body:
Probation raises practical judgement calls, and the right answer often depends on timing, evidence and openness. Four patterns recur.

First, a mistake. The best response is to report it promptly, explain what happened without excuses, fix what can be fixed, and say what you will do differently. A mistake handled this way is usually recorded as learning. A mistake hidden and found later is recorded as a conduct or honesty concern.

Second, a gap in support. If objectives are unclear, one-to-ones do not happen or training is missing, raise it early with your manager, in writing if necessary, and keep a record. Probation is a two-way arrangement, and a manager who is told of a gap can fix it.

Third, health, disability or caring needs. You may ask for reasonable adjustments, and the employer must consider them under the Equality Act 2010. Raising a need is not a sign of unsuitability. Absence during probation should be reported according to the department's rules, and managers should treat it fairly.

Fourth, disagreement. If you disagree with feedback, ask for examples, respond calmly, and record your view. If you disagree with a decision to extend or end probation, use the review or appeal route. Do not ignore it or react publicly.

Two cross-cutting habits help. Keep short notes of key conversations, and check the facts before you react. Probation decisions are made on evidence, and a record that shows steady, honest progress is the best protection.

If you are worried about conduct by others, the Code route applies, and you should not be penalised for raising a concern properly.

questions.prompt: You discover on Tuesday that a wrong figure went to a customer on Monday. What is the best response?

options.text: Blame the system you used, since the wrong figure came from its output and not from your own typing
Tell your manager now, explain what happened, and help to correct it
Say nothing for the time being, since the customer has not noticed that the figure is wrong
Wait until Friday so that you can try to fix it first without troubling your manager or the customer

questions.hint: Prompt, honest handling is recorded as learning.

questions.prompt: How is a hidden mistake that is found later likely to be treated?

options.text: As a development opportunity, since the person has now learned
As a matter for the customer only
As a minor issue, since all mistakes are treated alike
As a conduct or honesty concern in addition to the mistake

questions.hint: Concealment compounds the issue.
